case_info.scenario: A 13-year-old male presented with a 7-month history of a painless, progressively enlarging mass in the right parotid region. He underwent surgery at a local hospital 6 months prior. The pathological diagnosis was lymphadenitis. However, the mass persistently enlarged after the surgery. When the patient visited our hospital, a bulging mass (approximately 5 × 4 cm) was palpable in the right parotid region, which was firm, nontender, and immobile. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial computed tomography showed an ill-defined 3.6 × 3.2 × 2.7-cm soft-tissue mass in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland, with indistinct borders at the posterior margin of the right masseter muscle. Multiple mildly enlarged lymph nodes were noted at the inferior pole of the parotid gland and adjacent to the superior margin of the lesion (Figure 1A). The patient underwent right parotid mass resection and total parotidectomy with facial nerve dissection. Intraoperative findings indicated a firm mass located within the superficial parotid lobe. It had adhered to the surface of the mandibular ramus, with indistinct planes of dissection from the masseter and temporalis muscles. Histopathology results demonstrated that a circumscribed mass was surrounded by a thick fibrous pseudocapsule, and the tumor was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces and a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff were noted. The tumor showed focal sclerosing changes and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells appeared as mild atypia, while mitoses were rarely identified (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1 positivity.

case_info.explanation: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain differentiation that predominantly occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the extremities in children and adolescents, followed by the trunk and the head and neck regions.1Most cases arise in areas where lymph nodes are normally found, such as the antecubital fossa, inguinal area, supraclavicular fossa, and neck. Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. This case involved the right parotid region, an area rich in lymph nodes. The tissue resected during the initial surgery was in fact a lymph node, and the initial pathology diagnosis was lymphadenitis with marked lymphoid hyperplasia, follicular dendritic cell hyperplasia, and abundant plasma cell infiltration. Noticeably, the main lesion was not excised in this first procedure. The second surgery in our hospital successfully removed both the primary lesion and the surrounding lymph nodes. Morphologically, a circumscribed mass contained a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. The tumor nodule was surrounded by a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces containing blood and hemosiderin deposition were noted. The tumor represented focal hyalinized sclerosing stroma, marked inflammatory background, and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells manifested moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, and mildly atypical vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures were rarely identified. Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, EMA, ALK D5F3, vimentin, and KP-1 positivity of the tumor cells. Surprisingly, results also exhibited diffuse strong positivity for cyclin D1. The lymph nodes from the second operation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of AFH, later confirmed by molecular studies. The majority of AFHs harborEWSR1::CREB1fusion.3Less commonly,EWSR1::ATF1fusion is detected, which is more frequently associated with AFH of extrasomatic soft tissues.2The fluorescence in situ hybridization and targeted RNA sequencing revealed that the present patient had anEWSR1::ATF1fusion. These results confirmed the diagnosis of AFH. AFH is a neoplasm of rare metastasizing potential, predominantly to locoregional lymph nodes.4The lymph nodes excised during the patient’s second surgery showed no evidence of disease. However, on a retrospective review of the initial specimen, we identified sheets of spindle cells within the lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry results demonstrated that these cells were positive for desmin, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1, indicating nodal metastasis. The initial pathological diagnosis overlooked this finding, likely attributable to the rarity of this tumor and absence of histological context from the primary tumor. We report a rare case of AFH in the parotid region with metastasis to the lymph node. Reported cases indicate that AFH in the head and neck region may also occur in the mandible5and submandibular region.6Oral and maxillofacial surgeons and pathologists must include this rare entity in the differential diagnosis with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.7Immunophenotypic profiling and gene rearrangement detection serve as valuable ancillary diagnostic tools. Interestingly, the present case showed diffuse positivity of cyclin D1. While cyclin D1 is not classically associated with AFH, its expression in this case might raise questions regarding diagnostic specificity and deserves further investigation. This finding further suggests that AFH might share immunophenotype with other cyclin D1–positive spindle cell neoplasms, such as solitary fibrous tumor8and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.9The patient demonstrated no evidence of disease recurrence at the 5-month postoperative follow-up.

case_info.explanation: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain differentiation that predominantly occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the extremities in children and adolescents, followed by the trunk and the head and neck regions.1Most cases arise in areas where lymph nodes are normally found, such as the antecubital fossa, inguinal area, supraclavicular fossa, and neck. Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. This case involved the right parotid region, an area rich in lymph nodes. The tissue resected during the initial surgery was in fact a lymph node, and the initial pathology diagnosis was lymphadenitis with marked lymphoid hyperplasia, follicular dendritic cell hyperplasia, and abundant plasma cell infiltration. Noticeably, the main lesion was not excised in this first procedure. The second surgery in our hospital successfully removed both the primary lesion and the surrounding lymph nodes. Morphologically, a circumscribed mass contained a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. The tumor nodule was surrounded by a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces containing blood and hemosiderin deposition were noted. The tumor represented focal hyalinized sclerosing stroma, marked inflammatory background, and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells manifested moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, and mildly atypical vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures were rarely identified. Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, EMA, ALK D5F3, vimentin, and KP-1 positivity of the tumor cells. Surprisingly, results also exhibited diffuse strong positivity for cyclin D1. The lymph nodes from the second operation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of AFH, later confirmed by molecular studies. The majority of AFHs harborEWSR1::CREB1fusion.3Less commonly,EWSR1::ATF1fusion is detected, which is more frequently associated with AFH of extrasomatic soft tissues.2The fluorescence in situ hybridization and targeted RNA sequencing revealed that the present patient had anEWSR1::ATF1fusion. These results confirmed the diagnosis of AFH. AFH is a neoplasm of rare metastasizing potential, predominantly to locoregional lymph nodes.4The lymph nodes excised during the patient’s second surgery showed no evidence of disease. However, on a retrospective review of the initial specimen, we identified sheets of spindle cells within the lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry results demonstrated that these cells were positive for desmin, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1, indicating nodal metastasis. The initial pathological diagnosis overlooked this finding, likely attributable to the rarity of this tumor and absence of histological context from the primary tumor. We report a rare case of AFH in the parotid region with metastasis to the lymph node. Reported cases indicate that AFH in the head and neck region may also occur in the mandible5and submandibular region.6Oral and maxillofacial surgeons and pathologists must include this rare entity in the differential diagnosis with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.7Immunophenotypic profiling and gene rearrangement detection serve as valuable ancillary diagnostic tools. Interestingly, the present case showed diffuse positivity of cyclin D1. While cyclin D1 is not classically associated with AFH, its expression in this case might raise questions regarding diagnostic specificity and deserves further investigation. This finding further suggests that AFH might share immunophenotype with other cyclin D1–positive spindle cell neoplasms, such as solitary fibrous tumor8and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.9The patient demonstrated no evidence of disease recurrence at the 5-month postoperative follow-up.

case_info.explanation: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain differentiation that predominantly occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the extremities in children and adolescents, followed by the trunk and the head and neck regions.1Most cases arise in areas where lymph nodes are normally found, such as the antecubital fossa, inguinal area, supraclavicular fossa, and neck. Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. This case involved the right parotid region, an area rich in lymph nodes. The tissue resected during the initial surgery was in fact a lymph node, and the initial pathology diagnosis was lymphadenitis with marked lymphoid hyperplasia, follicular dendritic cell hyperplasia, and abundant plasma cell infiltration. Noticeably, the main lesion was not excised in this first procedure. The second surgery in our hospital successfully removed both the primary lesion and the surrounding lymph nodes. Morphologically, a circumscribed mass contained a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. The tumor nodule was surrounded by a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces containing blood and hemosiderin deposition were noted. The tumor represented focal hyalinized sclerosing stroma, marked inflammatory background, and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells manifested moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, and mildly atypical vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures were rarely identified. Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, EMA, ALK D5F3, vimentin, and KP-1 positivity of the tumor cells. Surprisingly, results also exhibited diffuse strong positivity for cyclin D1. The lymph nodes from the second operation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of AFH, later confirmed by molecular studies. The majority of AFHs harborEWSR1::CREB1fusion.3Less commonly,EWSR1::ATF1fusion is detected, which is more frequently associated with AFH of extrasomatic soft tissues.2The fluorescence in situ hybridization and targeted RNA sequencing revealed that the present patient had anEWSR1::ATF1fusion. These results confirmed the diagnosis of AFH. AFH is a neoplasm of rare metastasizing potential, predominantly to locoregional lymph nodes.4The lymph nodes excised during the patient’s second surgery showed no evidence of disease. However, on a retrospective review of the initial specimen, we identified sheets of spindle cells within the lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry results demonstrated that these cells were positive for desmin, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1, indicating nodal metastasis. The initial pathological diagnosis overlooked this finding, likely attributable to the rarity of this tumor and absence of histological context from the primary tumor. We report a rare case of AFH in the parotid region with metastasis to the lymph node. Reported cases indicate that AFH in the head and neck region may also occur in the mandible5and submandibular region.6Oral and maxillofacial surgeons and pathologists must include this rare entity in the differential diagnosis with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.7Immunophenotypic profiling and gene rearrangement detection serve as valuable ancillary diagnostic tools. Interestingly, the present case showed diffuse positivity of cyclin D1. While cyclin D1 is not classically associated with AFH, its expression in this case might raise questions regarding diagnostic specificity and deserves further investigation. This finding further suggests that AFH might share immunophenotype with other cyclin D1–positive spindle cell neoplasms, such as solitary fibrous tumor8and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.9The patient demonstrated no evidence of disease recurrence at the 5-month postoperative follow-up.

case_info.explanation: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain differentiation that predominantly occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the extremities in children and adolescents, followed by the trunk and the head and neck regions.1Most cases arise in areas where lymph nodes are normally found, such as the antecubital fossa, inguinal area, supraclavicular fossa, and neck. Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. case_info.explanation: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain differentiation that predominantly occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the extremities in children and adolescents, followed by the trunk and the head and neck regions.1Most cases arise in areas where lymph nodes are normally found, such as the antecubital fossa, inguinal area, supraclavicular fossa, and neck. Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. This case involved the right parotid region, an area rich in lymph nodes. The tissue resected during the initial surgery was in fact a lymph node, and the initial pathology diagnosis was lymphadenitis with marked lymphoid hyperplasia, follicular dendritic cell hyperplasia, and abundant plasma cell infiltration. Noticeably, the main lesion was not excised in this first procedure. The second surgery in our hospital successfully removed both the primary lesion and the surrounding lymph nodes. Morphologically, a circumscribed mass contained a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. The tumor nodule was surrounded by a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces containing blood and hemosiderin deposition were noted. The tumor represented focal hyalinized sclerosing stroma, marked inflammatory background, and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells manifested moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, and mildly atypical vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures were rarely identified. Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, EMA, ALK D5F3, vimentin, and KP-1 positivity of the tumor cells. Surprisingly, results also exhibited diffuse strong positivity for cyclin D1. The lymph nodes from the second operation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of AFH, later confirmed by molecular studies. The majority of AFHs harborEWSR1::CREB1fusion.3Less commonly,EWSR1::ATF1fusion is detected, which is more frequently associated with AFH of extrasomatic soft tissues.2The fluorescence in situ hybridization and targeted RNA sequencing revealed that the present patient had anEWSR1::ATF1fusion. These results confirmed the diagnosis of AFH. AFH is a neoplasm of rare metastasizing potential, predominantly to locoregional lymph nodes.4The lymph nodes excised during the patient’s second surgery showed no evidence of disease. However, on a retrospective review of the initial specimen, we identified sheets of spindle cells within the lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry results demonstrated that these cells were positive for desmin, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1, indicating nodal metastasis. The initial pathological diagnosis overlooked this finding, likely attributable to the rarity of this tumor and absence of histological context from the primary tumor. We report a rare case of AFH in the parotid region with metastasis to the lymph node. Reported cases indicate that AFH in the head and neck region may also occur in the mandible5and submandibular region.6Oral and maxillofacial surgeons and pathologists must include this rare entity in the differential diagnosis with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.7Immunophenotypic profiling and gene rearrangement detection serve as valuable ancillary diagnostic tools. Interestingly, the present case showed diffuse positivity of cyclin D1. While cyclin D1 is not classically associated with AFH, its expression in this case might raise questions regarding diagnostic specificity and deserves further investigation. This finding further suggests that AFH might share immunophenotype with other cyclin D1–positive spindle cell neoplasms, such as solitary fibrous tumor8and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.9The patient demonstrated no evidence of disease recurrence at the 5-month postoperative follow-up.

case_info.explanation: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain differentiation that predominantly occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the extremities in children and adolescents, followed by the trunk and the head and neck regions.1Most cases arise in areas where lymph nodes are normally found, such as the antecubital fossa, inguinal area, supraclavicular fossa, and neck. Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. This case involved the right parotid region, an area rich in lymph nodes. The tissue resected during the initial surgery was in fact a lymph node, and the initial pathology diagnosis was lymphadenitis with marked lymphoid hyperplasia, follicular dendritic cell hyperplasia, and abundant plasma cell infiltration. Noticeably, the main lesion was not excised in this first procedure. The second surgery in our hospital successfully removed both the primary lesion and the surrounding lymph nodes. Morphologically, a circumscribed mass contained a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. The tumor nodule was surrounded by a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces containing blood and hemosiderin deposition were noted. The tumor represented focal hyalinized sclerosing stroma, marked inflammatory background, and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells manifested moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, and mildly atypical vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures were rarely identified. Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, EMA, ALK D5F3, vimentin, and KP-1 positivity of the tumor cells. Surprisingly, results also exhibited diffuse strong positivity for cyclin D1. The lymph nodes from the second operation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of AFH, later confirmed by molecular studies. The majority of AFHs harborEWSR1::CREB1fusion.3Less commonly,EWSR1::ATF1fusion is detected, which is more frequently associated with AFH of extrasomatic soft tissues.2The fluorescence in situ hybridization and targeted RNA sequencing revealed that the present patient had anEWSR1::ATF1fusion. These results confirmed the diagnosis of AFH. AFH is a neoplasm of rare metastasizing potential, predominantly to locoregional lymph nodes.4The lymph nodes excised during the patient’s second surgery showed no evidence of disease. However, on a retrospective review of the initial specimen, we identified sheets of spindle cells within the lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry results demonstrated that these cells were positive for desmin, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1, indicating nodal metastasis. The initial pathological diagnosis overlooked this finding, likely attributable to the rarity of this tumor and absence of histological context from the primary tumor. We report a rare case of AFH in the parotid region with metastasis to the lymph node. Reported cases indicate that AFH in the head and neck region may also occur in the mandible5and submandibular region.6Oral and maxillofacial surgeons and pathologists must include this rare entity in the differential diagnosis with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.7Immunophenotypic profiling and gene rearrangement detection serve as valuable ancillary diagnostic tools. Interestingly, the present case showed diffuse positivity of cyclin D1. While cyclin D1 is not classically associated with AFH, its expression in this case might raise questions regarding diagnostic specificity and deserves further investigation. This finding further suggests that AFH might share immunophenotype with other cyclin D1–positive spindle cell neoplasms, such as solitary fibrous tumor8and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.9The patient demonstrated no evidence of disease recurrence at the 5-month postoperative follow-up.

Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. This case involved the right parotid region, an area rich in lymph nodes. The tissue resected during the initial surgery was in fact a lymph node, and the initial pathology diagnosis was lymphadenitis with marked lymphoid hyperplasia, follicular dendritic cell hyperplasia, and abundant plasma cell infiltration. Noticeably, the main lesion was not excised in this first procedure. The second surgery in our hospital successfully removed both the primary lesion and the surrounding lymph nodes. Morphologically, a circumscribed mass contained a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. The tumor nodule was surrounded by a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces containing blood and hemosiderin deposition were noted. The tumor represented focal hyalinized sclerosing stroma, marked inflammatory background, and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells manifested moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, and mildly atypical vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures were rarely identified. Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, EMA, ALK D5F3, vimentin, and KP-1 positivity of the tumor cells. Surprisingly, results also exhibited diffuse strong positivity for cyclin D1. The lymph nodes from the second operation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of AFH, later confirmed by molecular studies. The majority of AFHs harborEWSR1::CREB1fusion.3Less commonly,EWSR1::ATF1fusion is detected, which is more frequently associated with AFH of extrasomatic soft tissues.2The fluorescence in situ hybridization and targeted RNA sequencing revealed that the present patient had anEWSR1::ATF1fusion. These results confirmed the diagnosis of AFH. AFH is a neoplasm of rare metastasizing potential, predominantly to locoregional lymph nodes.4The lymph nodes excised during the patient’s second surgery showed no evidence of disease. However, on a retrospective review of the initial specimen, we identified sheets of spindle cells within the lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry results demonstrated that these cells were positive for desmin, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1, indicating nodal metastasis. We report a rare case of AFH in the parotid region with metastasis to the lymph node. Reported cases indicate that AFH in the head and neck region may also occur in the mandible5and submandibular region.6Oral and maxillofacial surgeons and pathologists must include this rare entity in the differential diagnosis with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.7Immunophenotypic profiling and gene rearrangement detection serve as valuable ancillary diagnostic tools. Interestingly, the present case showed diffuse positivity of cyclin D1. case_info.explanation: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain differentiation that predominantly occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the extremities in children and adolescents, followed by the trunk and the head and neck regions.1Most cases arise in areas where lymph nodes are normally found, such as the antecubital fossa, inguinal area, supraclavicular fossa, and neck. Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. This case involved the right parotid region, an area rich in lymph nodes. The tissue resected during the initial surgery was in fact a lymph node, and the initial pathology diagnosis was lymphadenitis with marked lymphoid hyperplasia, follicular dendritic cell hyperplasia, and abundant plasma cell infiltration. Noticeably, the main lesion was not excised in this first procedure. The second surgery in our hospital successfully removed both the primary lesion and the surrounding lymph nodes. Morphologically, a circumscribed mass contained a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. The tumor nodule was surrounded by a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces containing blood and hemosiderin deposition were noted. The tumor represented focal hyalinized sclerosing stroma, marked inflammatory background, and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells manifested moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, and mildly atypical vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures were rarely identified. Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, EMA, ALK D5F3, vimentin, and KP-1 positivity of the tumor cells. Surprisingly, results also exhibited diffuse strong positivity for cyclin D1. The lymph nodes from the second operation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of AFH, later confirmed by molecular studies. The majority of AFHs harborEWSR1::CREB1fusion.3Less commonly,EWSR1::ATF1fusion is detected, which is more frequently associated with AFH of extrasomatic soft tissues.2The fluorescence in situ hybridization and targeted RNA sequencing revealed that the present patient had anEWSR1::ATF1fusion. These results confirmed the diagnosis of AFH. AFH is a neoplasm of rare metastasizing potential, predominantly to locoregional lymph nodes.4The lymph nodes excised during the patient’s second surgery showed no evidence of disease. However, on a retrospective review of the initial specimen, we identified sheets of spindle cells within the lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry results demonstrated that these cells were positive for desmin, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1, indicating nodal metastasis. The initial pathological diagnosis overlooked this finding, likely attributable to the rarity of this tumor and absence of histological context from the primary tumor. We report a rare case of AFH in the parotid region with metastasis to the lymph node. Reported cases indicate that AFH in the head and neck region may also occur in the mandible5and submandibular region.6Oral and maxillofacial surgeons and pathologists must include this rare entity in the differential diagnosis with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.7Immunophenotypic profiling and gene rearrangement detection serve as valuable ancillary diagnostic tools. Interestingly, the present case showed diffuse positivity of cyclin D1. While cyclin D1 is not classically associated with AFH, its expression in this case might raise questions regarding diagnostic specificity and deserves further investigation. This finding further suggests that AFH might share immunophenotype with other cyclin D1–positive spindle cell neoplasms, such as solitary fibrous tumor8and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.9The patient demonstrated no evidence of disease recurrence at the 5-month postoperative follow-up.
